title: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in pkg/rootless/rootless_linux.c
body:
### Issue Description

While testing Podman built with AddressSanitizer, I found a heap-buffer-overflow in `do_preexec_hooks_dir()` (`rootless_linux.c`) when using the preexec-hooks mechanism.

The issue is caused by an off-by-one write after incrementing `nfiles`:

```c
strncpy(buffer + nfiles * (NAME_MAX + 1),
        de->d_name,
        NAME_MAX + 1);

nfiles++;
buffer[nfiles * (NAME_MAX + 1)] = '\0';

### Steps to reproduce the issue

## Steps to reproduce the issue

1. Build Podman with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer enabled:

```bash
CGO_CFLAGS="-g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined" \
CGO_LDFLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined" \
go build -o podman_asan ./cmd/podman
```

2. Create a directory with several fake preexec hooks:

```bash
mkdir /tmp/hooks
for i in $(seq 1 5); do
    touch /tmp/hooks/h$i.sh
done
```

3. Force Podman to detect the preexec hooks configuration by either:
   - creating `/etc/containers/podman_preexec_hooks.txt`, or
   - using the following `LD_PRELOAD` library:

```c
#define _GNU_SOURCE
#include <dlfcn.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <unistd.h>

static int (*real_access)(const char *, int);

int access(const char *pathname, int mode)
{
    if (!real_access)
        real_access = dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "access");

    if (strcmp(pathname,
               "/etc/containers/podman_preexec_hooks.txt") == 0)
        return 0;

    return real_access(pathname, mode);
}
```

Build the library:

```bash
gcc -shared -fPIC fake_access.c -o fake_access.so -ldl
```

4. Run Podman with the fake hooks directory:

```bash
ASAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1:detect_leaks=0 \
PODMAN_PREEXEC_HOOKS_DIR=/tmp/hooks \
LD_PRELOAD="/usr/lib64/libasan.so.8 /path/to/fake_access.so" \
./podman_asan version
```

AddressSanitizer reports a heap-buffer-overflow in `do_preexec_hooks_dir()`.

### Describe the results you expected

```markdown
No out-of-bounds memory accesses should occur.

The extra null-byte write should either be removed or the allocation should reserve space for an additional entry if a sentinel element is intended.

### Additional information

The heap-buffer-overflow is caused by the following code:

```c
buffer = realloc(buffer, (nfiles + 1) * (NAME_MAX + 1));

...

strncpy(buffer + nfiles * (NAME_MAX + 1),
        de->d_name,
        NAME_MAX + 1);

nfiles++;
buffer[nfiles * (NAME_MAX + 1)] = '\0';
```

`realloc()` allocates space for exactly `(nfiles + 1)` entries of size
`NAME_MAX + 1` bytes.

For the first file (`nfiles == 0`), the allocation size is 256 bytes
(assuming `NAME_MAX == 255`), with valid indices in the range `[0, 255]`.

After copying the filename, `nfiles` is incremented:

```c
nfiles++;
```

The subsequent write

```c
buffer[nfiles * (NAME_MAX + 1)] = '\0';
```

becomes

```c
buffer[256] = '\0';
```

which writes one byte past the end of the allocated buffer.

This extra write also appears to be unnecessary. According to the POSIX
specification, `readdir()` returns a null-terminated filename in
`dirent::d_name` whose length does not exceed `NAME_MAX`. Therefore,

```c
strncpy(buffer + nfiles * (NAME_MAX + 1),
        de->d_name,
        NAME_MAX + 1);
```

already copies the terminating `'\0'` into the destination buffer.

If the intention was to append an additional empty sentinel entry after the
last filename, the allocation should reserve space for one more
`NAME_MAX + 1` byte slot. Otherwise, the explicit null-byte write should be
removed.

This issue was found during internal security testing at ALT Linux Team.
